content: Sexual health is a critical component of physical, emotional, and social well-being for individuals, couples, and families. It also plays a significant role in the social and economic development of communities and nations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines sexual health as a state of physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being in relation to sexuality. It is not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction, or infirmity. Achieving sexual health requires a positive and respectful approach to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the ability to have pleasurable and safe sexual experiences free of coercion, discrimination, and violence. Unsafe sexual practices and violations of human rights related to sexuality, such as sexual coercion, contribute significantly to the global burden of disease. These issues highlight the importance of addressing sexual health as a public health priority. Over the past decades, research and consultations have identified sexuality-related communication as an area requiring urgent attention. While many clients desire discussions about sexual health with their healthcare providers, many health workers lack the training and knowledge to address these concerns effectively. This gap underscores the need for clear guidance on the role of sexuality communication in primary care. In 2008, WHO commissioned case studies to explore the integration of sexuality counseling into sexual and reproductive health services. These studies served as a foundation for the development of this guideline. In 2010, an expert consultation convened by WHO’s Department of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) recommended the creation of a guideline to facilitate the integration of sexuality counseling into primary care services. This initiative aims to ensure that healthcare providers incorporate brief sexuality-related communication (BSC) into sexual and reproductive health services. By initiating such discussions, health workers can promote sexual health rather than solely addressing negative health outcomes such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), HIV, sexual violence, harmful practices like female genital mutilation (FGM), and unintended pregnancies. The guideline development process began in 2012 with the establishment of a Guideline Development Group (GDG) composed of experts in sexual health from lowand middle-income countries across all WHO regions. The group included academics, psychologists, physicians, public health specialists, lawyers, and social scientists with expertise in developing programs or providing clinical services to promote sexual health and well-being. Representatives of key constituencies with overlapping sexual health and rights expertise were also included. Under the GDG’s guidance, a systematic review was conducted, and evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. The GDG developed one good practice recommendation and two policy recommendations based on the systematic review, expert input, and peer reviews. These recommendations aim to provide health policymakers and decision-makers in health professional training institutions with advice on the rationale for using counseling skills to address sexual health concerns in primary care settings. The ultimate goal is to improve the quality of sexual health care and the training of healthcare providers in BSC knowledge and skills. BSC is recommended for the prevention of sexually transmitted infections among adults and adolescents in primary health services. The quality of evidence supporting this recommendation is low to moderate, but the strength of the recommendation is strong. Training healthcare providers in sexual health knowledge and BSC skills is also strongly recommended, despite the low to very low quality of evidence. These recommendations emphasize the importance of respecting, protecting, and fulfilling clients’ human rights when implementing BSC in health services. The guideline document also highlights the need for WHO to develop and test specific BSC techniques to guide healthcare providers in improving the quality of care. This initiative represents an initial step toward ensuring that healthcare providers integrate BSC into sexual and reproductive health services. By doing so, they can address a broader range of sexual health concerns and promote overall well-being.
